title: Sentence Rearrangement and Sentence Structure
shortDescription: Putting jumbled parts back into logical order, plus the basic subject-verb-object skeleton every sentence is built on.
genZNote: A jumbled sentence is a puzzle with a start piece and connector clues — find those two and the rest falls into place.

rows: Two+ independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction
She reads novels, and he watches films.
One independent clause + one or more dependent clauses
Although it was raining, she went for a walk.
Two+ independent clauses + at least one dependent clause
She went for a walk although it was raining, and he stayed home.

sections.heading: Clues for solving jumbled sentence / paragraph questions
bullets: Find the STARTER — the sentence that introduces the subject/topic without relying on a pronoun that refers back to something not yet mentioned; a sentence starting with 'This', 'It', 'He/She/They', 'However', or 'Therefore' is rarely the opening line.
Match PRONOUNS to their antecedents — a sentence using 'he' must come after the sentence that first names that person.
Follow CHRONOLOGY and CAUSE-EFFECT — an effect sentence must follow its cause sentence; a 'first...then...finally' sequence has an obvious internal order.
Use CONNECTOR WORDS as glue — 'however', 'therefore', 'in addition', 'for example' each signal a specific relationship to the sentence immediately before them.
Once you find a confirmed PAIR of sentences that must go together, treat that pair as a single block — this quickly narrows down the full order.

sections.heading: Phrase vs clause — the small distinction behind structure questions
sections.body: A CLAUSE has both a subject and a verb ('because it was raining'); a PHRASE does not ('in spite of the rain'). Recognising this helps identify sentence type (simple/complex) and helps in error-detection questions that hinge on whether a group of words needs a comma, a conjunction, or is already a complete clause on its own.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Sentences are built from clauses in one of four patterns (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex); jumbled-sentence questions are solved by finding the true opening line, then following pronoun and connector clues.
keyFacts: A sentence opening with 'This/It/He/She/They/However/Therefore' is rarely the true first sentence of a jumbled set.
A clause has a subject + verb; a phrase does not.
Connector words (however, therefore, for example) signal the exact logical link to the previous sentence.

highYieldFacts: Finding one confirmed pronoun-antecedent pair often cracks open the entire rearrangement order.
commonTraps: Picking a sentence with a pronoun or connector as the opening line.
Ignoring chronological/cause-effect order in favour of only checking grammar.
mustRemember: Identify the true starter sentence first; everything else locks into place around it.
possibleQuestions: Arrange the jumbled sentences (P, Q, R, S) to form a coherent paragraph.
Identify the sentence type: 'Although he was late, he still managed to finish the race, and his team celebrated.'
